meaning.text: The meaning of the word Yaga is uncertain.
Afanasyev holds that the word yaga answers to the Sanskrit ahi, "snake".
Shchepkin, as quoted by Ralston, says Yaga means properly "noisy, scolding", from a root yagat', to brawl or scold.

appearance.text: Is generally represented under the form of an old woman.
Her nose is sometimes described as being of iron.
Her long nose is described as snotty.
Has long pendant breasts, sometimes described as being of iron.
Has strong sharp teeth, sometimes described as being of iron.
In the epic description of the tales she has a bony leg.
As she lies in her hut she often stretches across from one corner to the other, and her nose goes right through the ceiling.
As she lies in her hut her breasts hang down over the shelf-rail.

scene.text: Her usual dwelling is a cottage that stands on fowls' legs, that is, on slender supports.
The hut stands at the edge of a forest, with its entrance looking towards the forest.
Sometimes she lives in a larger building, round which stands a fence made of the bones of the people she has eaten, tipped with their skulls.
The uprights of the gates of that building are human legs, the bolts are human arms, and instead of a lock there is a mouth with sharp teeth.
In some places, when the wind bows down the ears of corn, the peasants say that the Baba Yaga is running after children.

behavior_habitat.text: The White-Russians declare that the Baba Yaga flies through the sky in a fiery mortar, which she urges on with a burning broom.
During her flight the winds howl, the earth groans, and the trees writhe and crack.
The White-Russians affirm that Death gives the dead to the Baba Yaga, and that Death often goes prowling about with her.
The White-Russians affirm that the Baba Yaga and her subordinate witches feed on the souls of people, and by that means become as light as spirits.

appearance.text: The Serbs' gvozdenzuba is a woman with iron teeth.

behavior_habitat.text: The Servian Baba Yaga, known as the Iron Tooth, carries about live coals in a pitcher.
The Iron Tooth burns the distaffs of lazy spinners.
The Serbs frighten naughty girls and boys with the gvozdenzuba.
In a Slovak tale the sons of a Baba Yaga are described as baneful snakes.
The Slovaks believe that the baba-yaga can send foul weather and fair weather at her own will.
The Little Russians, forbidding children to pick peas, tell them not to go into the peas because the iron baba sits there.
With the same threat they stop children from running into the woods and gardens.
She is the most prominent of the mythic personages in the popular tales (skazki).
When she goes abroad she rides in an iron mortar, which she propels with the pestle.
As she goes she sweeps away the traces of her passage with a broom.
She flies through the air and rides to the witches' sabbaths in an iron mortar.
According to some stories the Sun, the Day and the Night are her servants.
According to some stories trunkless hands wait upon her and the elements fulfil her behests.
She possesses a magic cudgel, a single wave of which turns any living creature into stone.
She can always avail herself of fire-breathing horses, seven-league boots, self-playing gusli, a self-cutting sword and a self-flying carpet.
She cooks and eats her victims, often stealing children and belated travellers for her table.
As a general rule she is described as utterly malevolent and always hungering after human flesh.
It is also told that the baba-yaga steals children, lifts them into the air and throws them down dead onto the roof of the house.
The baba-yaga and the witches sense the presence of a hidden man, and on meeting wandering heroes exclaim that a Russian smell is here.
She is supposed to love to suck the white breasts of beautiful women.
She keeps guard over, and knows the use of, the founts of Living Water, which cure wounds and restore the dead to life.
She carefully hides copper, silver and gold in her store-rooms.
Different versions of the same tale sometimes give the leading part to the Snake and sometimes to the Baba Yaga.
Sometimes three Baba Yagas appear in a story; they are usually three sisters, not of an unkindly nature, who give the hero good advice and magic presents.
In some places the peasants say she runs after children in the corn with the intention of blinding them or pounding them in an iron churn.
Corn-fields are specially haunted by the Baba Yaga.
In the Poshekhonsky district peasants frighten children away from running over the kitchen-gardens and fields with the baba-yaga.
She is frequently represented as spinning.
According to popular traditions she spins tow, weaves linen, and chases her victims with an iron comb in her hands.
She usually lives by herself, but sometimes appears in the character of the house-mother.
In one story she petrifies her victims: she gives a hero one of her hairs and tells him to tie three knots and blow, and he and his horse turn into stone.
In that story she puts the petrified victims in her mortar, pounds them to bits, and buries the remains under a stone.
From the Christmas-season games Afanasyev concludes that she is a master at setting riddles and solving them.

dealing_with_it.text: When her hut is adjured in the right words it turns round, so that its back is towards the forest and its front towards the person addressing it.
In one story Prince Ivan feigns ignorance and persuades her to show him how to tie the knots and blow, so that she petrifies herself.
Prince Ivan then pounds her in her own mortar until she tells him where his comrade's fragments are and how to restore him to life.
In one tale two heroes lie in wait for her, catch her, and force her to show them the spring of living water.

notes.text: origin: no opened page says where the Baba Yaga comes from or who becomes one. Ralston (ralston1872:pp.163-164) and Afanasyev (afanasyev1869:pp.587-595) give mythologists' readings (storm, whirlwind, thunder-cloud, degraded heathen prophetesses for the three sisters); these are interpretations, not lore, and were left out. Searched baba yaga, baba-yaga, yaga, jaga-baba, jezibaba, баба-яга, баба яга, яга, ягу in all sources.

Read in full: ralston1872:pp.161-164, ralston1873:pp.137-138 and p.147, afanasyev1869:pp.586-595, machal1918:p.266. Not opened for budget: ralston1873:pp.92-95, 125-126, 139-157 (tale texts, incl. Vasilissa at pp.152-157), 169-170, 248-250; afanasyev1865:pp.217, 291, 363, 569, 573, 775; afanasyev1868:pp.419, 449, 483, 595, 763, 780; afanasyev1869:pp.24, 451, 457, 459, 463, 467, 540-544; ralston1872:pp.168, 172, 373, 385. These tale pages may hold further scene detail and wards.

names.meaning clauses 1-2 come from Ralston's own footnote 3 on ralston1872:p.161, and the Shchepkin clause from footnote 2 on ralston1873:p.137; the Afanasyev etymology is in the body text of afanasyev1869:p.588. They are authors' statements about the name, not references.

Iron Tooth native form: afanasyev1869:p.595 prints 'сербская гвоздензуба' in its baba-yaga passage, and ralston1872:p.164 names the Servian Baba Yaga 'Iron Tooth' with the same coal-carrying, distaff-burning trait; the identification of the two rests on that parallel. Afanasyev p.592 prints the inflected form 'гвоздензубою'.

Related links: afanasyev1869:p.593 compares the baba-yaga hiding in the corn-fields with tales of mavki, rusalki and poludnitsy, hence rusalka and poludnitsa as 'related'. Ralston (ralston1872:p.162) and Afanasyev (p.588) tie her to 'the Snake' / 'Fiery Snake'; no opened page names Zmey Gorynych, so no zmey-gorynych link was made.

Sources call her 'hideous' (ralston1872:p.161) and 'evil, ugly' (afanasyev1869:p.591); these style words were kept out of appearance per the drawing rule. Afanasyev p.591's 'голова пестомъ' (head like a pestle?) was left out as its sense is unclear.

Ukrainian variant: afanasyev1869:p.591 ties the 'iron baba' (зализна баба) of the Little Russians to the baba-yaga, who is called 'iron' in Rus'. Ralston's 'In the Ukraine the flying witch is usually called a snake' (ralston1872:p.162) was not used, since it is about a witch, not this creature.
